CLIMATE NOTE

NOTE
A dry and stable airmass remains in place this morning after an extended period of clear skies and subsequent radiative cooling overnight. Temperatures have dropped into the low-mid 30s as of 3 AM, with another few hours of cooling expected to bring lows into the upper 20s in some spots. The decoupled boundary layer sits beneath ongoing WAA where h8 temperatures peak at 7-8 C, meaning as diurnal mixing erodes the inversion, temperatures climb into the mid 50s. Veering vertical wind profiles also show strengthening low level winds throughout the day, which the growing boundary layer will tap into to produce breezy WSW winds gusting to 30 mph during the daylight hours. Looking at GOES-19 satellite imagery, a band of mid-high cloud is accelerating eastward into Lower Michigan on the nose of a 90-95 knot upper level jet (noted as the dry slot in mid level WV imagery). This moisture corridor represents the lead edge of height falls associated with the mature stacked low over western Ontario, which sends a weak surface front across SE Michigan by early this afternoon. While the frontal passage itself will be dry, subsequent cold advection will add to the moisture pool by establishing moisture flux off of the lake aggregate. Hi-res models show a convergence signal over the Saginaw Valley/Thumb which could lead to shower activity across these portions of the forecast area, so long as lake effect bands do not set up entirely offshore. Elsewhere, stratus expands south for mostly cloudy skies overnight. Cloud cover and lake induced showers linger into Monday morning before moisture is scoured out by the brief influence of high pressure. Surface pressure during the first half of the week fluctuates between 1010-1020mb in a progressive, low amplitude pressure pattern. The weak nature of the waves has little impact on temperature prospects, with Tuesday actually being the warmest day of the period (highs in the low 60s) despite a surface trough passing through earlier in the day. Reliance on Pacific moisture just does not provide enough depth for any meaningful rain chances over land through Wednesday. A more pronounced pattern shift arrives late in the week as a much stronger low slides across the Ohio Valley, followed by colder Canadian air crashing in from the north. This could introduce our first shot at mixed precipitation with the arrival of the coldest air of the season. && .MARINE... Strengthening gradient flow materializes across the central Great Lakes today as the next low pressure system clips the northern waterways through early Monday. This initially supports breezy southwesterly winds with gusts peaking between 25 and 30 knots, considering the initial stable warm advection regime. However, as this low exits, winds will veer to the northwest behind the attendant cold front, ushering in the next dose of colder air. Instability then builds over the warmer lake waters which deepens mixing depths and taps into stronger flow above the lake surface. A Gale Warning remains in effect given the cold advection and consensus in lower column wind speeds. Gusts should hover near the gale threshold across the northern half of Lake Huron this evening through early Monday. Meanwhile, Small Craft Advisories are in effect for the southern Huron nearshores. Expect periods of gusts at/above 25 knots and waves in excess of 4 feet. Quick shifts to shortwave ridging Monday and then back to a troughing pattern with a dry frontal passage develops early next week, with lower potential to reach marine headline criteria. && .PREV DISCUSSION... Issued at 1154 PM EST Sat Nov 7 2026 AVIATION... Shortwave ridging aloft and a surge in westerlies will result in dry air advection across Southeast Michigan tonight. There is an overwhelming signal for active and lowering subsidence below 8.0 kft agl. Southwest gradient flow will increase substantially ahead of a weak cold front on Sunday. Some uncertainty exists on the coverage of boundary layer cloud early as model sounding show the layer of saturation to be very shallow. By late in the day, sharp cyclonic trough will bring a steep midlevel lapse rates to allow for some shower activity primarily in the Thumb and Lake Huron. DTW THRESHOLD PROBABILITIES... * Medium for ceiling 5000 ft Sunday afternoon and evening. && .DTX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES... MI...None. Lake Huron...Gale Warning from 4 PM this afternoon to 4 AM EST Monday for LHZ361- 362. Small Craft Advisory until 4 AM EST Monday for LHZ421-422. Small Craft Advisory from 10 AM this morning to 4 AM EST Monday for LHZ441>443. Lake St Clair...Small Craft Advisory from 7 AM this morning to 10 PM EST this evening for LCZ460. Michigan waters of Lake Erie...Small Craft Advisory from 7 AM this morning to 10 PM EST this evening for LEZ444. && $$ DISCUSSION...MV MARINE.......KGK AVIATION.....CB You can obtain your latest National Weather Service forecasts online at www.weather.gov/detroit.

.DISCUSSION...

A dry and stable airmass remains in place this morning after an 
extended period of clear skies and subsequent radiative cooling 
overnight. Temperatures have dropped into the low-mid 30s as of 3 
AM, with another few hours of cooling expected to bring lows into 
the upper 20s in some spots. The decoupled boundary layer sits 
beneath ongoing WAA where h8 temperatures peak at 7-8 C, meaning as 
diurnal mixing erodes the inversion, temperatures climb into the mid 
50s. Veering vertical wind profiles also show strengthening low 
level winds throughout the day, which the growing boundary layer 
will tap into to produce breezy WSW winds gusting to 30 mph during 
the daylight hours. 

Looking at GOES-19 satellite imagery, a band of mid-high cloud is 
accelerating eastward into Lower Michigan on the nose of a 90-95 
knot upper level jet (noted as the dry slot in mid level WV 
imagery). This moisture corridor represents the lead edge of height 
falls associated with the mature stacked low over western Ontario, 
which sends a weak surface front across SE Michigan by early this 
afternoon. While the frontal passage itself will be dry, subsequent 
cold advection will add to the moisture pool by establishing 
moisture flux off of the lake aggregate. Hi-res models show a 
convergence signal over the Saginaw Valley/Thumb which could lead to 
shower activity across these portions of the forecast area, so long 
as lake effect bands do not set up entirely offshore. Elsewhere, 
stratus expands south for mostly cloudy skies overnight. 

Cloud cover and lake induced showers linger into Monday morning 
before moisture is scoured out by the brief influence of high 
pressure. Surface pressure during the first half of the week 
fluctuates between 1010-1020mb in a progressive, low amplitude 
pressure pattern. The weak nature of the waves has little impact on 
temperature prospects, with Tuesday actually being the warmest day 
of the period (highs in the low 60s) despite a surface trough 
passing through earlier in the day. Reliance on Pacific moisture 
just does not provide enough depth for any meaningful rain chances 
over land through Wednesday. 

A more pronounced pattern shift arrives late in the week as a much 
stronger low slides across the Ohio Valley, followed by colder 
Canadian air crashing in from the north. This could introduce our 
first shot at mixed precipitation with the arrival of the coldest 
air of the season.

Instability then builds over the warmer lake waters which deepens
